# Hereditary inverse-power depth and the effective dimension of a cap cover

These are ordinary continuous theorems. They do not replace any mixed-integer sum by a projective integral.

Write gamma_0=1 and gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r for integers r>=1.

## 1. An attained depth theorem for inverse-power densities

Let r>=1, beta>=r+1, and let f be a finite positive-integral density on R^r, positive on an open full-dimensional convex set U and zero outside it. Suppose f^(-1/beta) is finite positive and convex on U. Let M=integral f. Then there is one point y in U such that every closed halfspace containing y has f-mass at least gamma_r M. The maximum depth is attained.

The inverse-power radial lemma, with its full proof and tail estimates, is Section 1 of `candidate 2338b9b22d6faa2f`. We spell out the remaining depth argument here.

For a unit normal u put G(y,u)=integral_{u.(x-y)>=0} f(x) dx. Hyperplanes have f-mass zero, so G is jointly continuous by dominated convergence. Its minimum over the compact sphere, D_f(y), is continuous. A halfspace with normal y/|y| through y lies outside the ball of radius |y|, so D_f(y) tends to zero as |y| tends to infinity. At an interior support point it is positive: a sufficiently small ball about that point has a positive lower density bound, and every containing halfspace captures at least half of that ball. Consequently a positive maximum Q is attained in a bounded set. A point outside U, including its boundary, has a separating or supporting containing halfspace of f-mass zero; a maximizer y therefore lies in U.

Let A={u:G(y,u)=Q}. This is a nonempty compact set of unit normals. Zero belongs to conv(A). Otherwise strict separation gives v and delta>0 such that u.v>=delta for all u in A. On a neighborhood N of A this remains at least delta/2. Moving y to y-epsilon v adds, for every u in N, a slab through a fixed small ball where f is bounded below. The added mass is at least c epsilon uniformly, so these cap masses exceed Q. On the compact complement of N the original masses exceed Q by a uniform positive amount, and joint continuity preserves this strict gap for small epsilon. All containing cap masses then exceed Q, a contradiction.

Caratheodory supplies finitely many active normals with positive weights summing to one and weighted normal sum zero. Their closed through-y halfspaces cover R^r: if a point belonged to none, all weighted scalar products would be negative, contradicting the zero sum.

Apply the proved inverse-power radial construction about y. It produces an r-dimensional convex body B of volume M, preserving EVERY through-y cap mass. The selected active caps cover B and all have B-volume Q. The ordinary centroid of B belongs to one of them. Ordinary Gruenbaum gives Q>=gamma_r M. The original maximizing y has the desired depth and belongs to the actual positive support.

If f is restricted to any closed convex set L with positive f-mass, it retains the same hypothesis after replacing its support by U intersect int(L). The discarded boundary has zero Lebesgue measure. The intersection is nonempty and full-dimensional because L has positive f-mass. Thus the conclusion is HEREDITARY under convex restriction, with the same gamma_r.

Log-concave densities are included: f^(-1/(r+1)) is convex on the positive support, as the exponential of the convex function -(log f)/(r+1).

## 2. Exact truncation for this density class

If finitely many halfspaces cover the support of a density in Section 1 and have masses A_i, then for every alpha>=0,

    sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/gamma_r >= M.              (1)

This is the abstract hereditary-depth distal-truncation argument in `candidate cd833c78fb705a2e`. Explicitly, trim from each cap with A_i>alpha an outer parallel cap of mass A_i-alpha. Continuous cap tails give the threshold. The convex remainder has mass at least M-sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+, and every original cap has mass at most alpha on it. If this remainder has positive mass, Section 1 applied to the restricted density and the fact that the original caps still cover it give gamma_r times its mass at most alpha. If the lower remainder bound is nonpositive, (1) is immediate.

## 3. General projective marginal calculation

Let K be a convex body in R^D. Suppose a nonconstant affine coordinate t is nonnegative on K, and use affine coordinates (v,t,y), v in R^r, y in R^(D-r-1), where 1<=r<=D-1. The pushforward of ordinary volume by z=v/t, ignoring the zero-volume t=0 boundary, has density

    F(z)=J integral_(t>0) integral_y 1_K(tz,t,y) t^r dy dt,

where J>0 is the fixed affine-coordinate Jacobian. It is integrable, bounded, and has full-dimensional convex positive support. With s=1/t and w=y/t this becomes

    F(z)=J integral 1_Omega(z,s,w) s^(-(D+1)) ds dw,

where Omega={(z,s,w):s>0,(z/s,1/s,w/s) in K} is convex. The Jacobian exponent is r+2+(D-r-1)=D+1. The integrand has convex power -1/(D+1), since that power is s on its convex support. There are D-r integrated variables. The standard BBL marginal theorem gives output exponent

    [-1/(D+1)]/[1-(D-r)/(D+1)]=-1/(r+1).

Thus F^(-1/(r+1)) is convex on its positive support. As usual pass to the open interior of that support, changing no integrals. The BBL input and primary reference are stated precisely in Section 3 of `candidate 2338b9b22d6faa2f`.

## 4. Sharp effective-dimension theorem for any finite cap cover

Let K be a convex body in R^D, D>=1, of volume V. Let m>=1 closed halfspaces cover K, with masses A_1,...,A_m. Set

    s=min{D,m-1}.

Then, for every alpha>=0,

    sum_(i=1)^m (A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/gamma_s >= V.         (2)

In particular

    sum_i A_i-V >= (m-1/gamma_s) min_i A_i.                (3)

The factor gamma_s is sharp for each D,m.

**Proof.** Choose an inclusion-minimal subcover of j<=m caps. If j=1, its mass is V and (2) follows directly from (V-alpha)_++alpha/gamma_s>=V. Assume j>=2. Let rho be the rank of its normals.

If rho<=j-1, orthogonally project uniform volume onto that rho-dimensional span. The cap masses and total mass are preserved. The marginal density is log-concave by ordinary Prekopa (equivalently the usual section-volume Brunn--Minkowski implication). Section 1 and then (1) give the cap-mass inequality with gamma_rho. Here rho<=min(D,j-1)<=s, so gamma_rho>=gamma_s. Enlarging the alpha coefficient to 1/gamma_s and restoring the other nonnegative summands proves (2).

It remains that rho=j, so the j cap margins give an affine map onto R^j. The image of K is a full-dimensional compact convex set disjoint from the open negative orthant. Separating these convex sets gives lambda_i>=0, not all zero, with sum lambda_i margin_i>=0 on K. Minimality of the subcover forces every lambda_i>0; otherwise the positive-coefficient caps alone cover K. Put t=sum lambda_i margin_i. This is a nonconstant affine coordinate, nonnegative on K and positive on int(K).

Choose the remaining coordinates so that the j margins are homogeneous linear functions of (v,t), with v in R^(j-1), and y in their common kernel. The projective map z=v/t sends each cap to an affine halfspace in R^(j-1), preserves its mass, and sends the cover to a cover of the entire plane R^(j-1): the positive weighted sum of its margin functions is identically one. Section 3 gives an inverse-power marginal with exponent -1/j. Section 1 therefore supplies the hereditary depth constant gamma_(j-1). Applying (1), then gamma_(j-1)>=gamma_s and restoring omitted caps, proves (2). Taking alpha=min_i A_i gives (3).

For sharpness, if m-1<=D, take a simplex T in dimension s=m-1 times any positive-volume convex body in the remaining dimensions, and use the m canonical simplex centroid caps. All masses equal gamma_s V and the caps cover the body. At alpha=gamma_s V, any larger proposed g in place of gamma_s would violate (2). If m-1>D, use the D+1 canonical caps of a D-simplex and add halfspaces disjoint from K until there are m; the same test alpha=gamma_D V proves sharpness. For m=1, a cap containing all of K gives gamma_0=1 directly, with no 0^0 convention.

## Limits of the result for OC

This is an ordinary continuous cap-cover theorem with an explicit positive-part profile. It applies to each measured integer fiber in its own affine hull. The normals may be oblique before restriction; a whole or empty fiber trace is an elementary case. The theorem does not provide one mixed-integer point, and the per-fiber cap orderings and truncation thresholds can differ. A global use must still control those differences while retaining the original lattice and original measure.
